title: Load Balancing Algorithms
description: Compare common load balancing algorithms including round-robin, least connections, and IP hash, and learn when each is appropriate.

data.text: A load balancing algorithm determines how incoming requests are distributed across backend servers. The choice of algorithm affects latency, server utilization, and failure behavior. Most systems default to round-robin, but more advanced algorithms can significantly improve performance under variable load.

Round robin distributes requests sequentially across a list of servers. It is simple and stateless, which makes it easy to implement and debug. However, it ignores server load and response time, so a slow server can still receive the same number of requests as a fast one.

data.title: Limitation
data.text: Round robin works best when servers have similar capacity and request costs. Under heterogeneous workloads, it can waste resources on overloaded or slower instances.

The least connections algorithm sends each new request to the server with the fewest active connections. This adapts better to long-lived connections and uneven processing times. It is commonly used for database proxies and application servers where request duration varies widely.

IP hash maps a client IP address to a specific server using a hash function. This improves session locality without storing explicit session state. The downside is that adding or removing servers changes the hash ring, which can cause session disruption during scaling events.

data.caption: How different load balancing algorithms route requests to backend servers.
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    Request -->|Round Robin| RR[Assign next server in list]
    Request -->|Least Connections| LC[Pick server with fewest connections]
    Request -->|IP Hash| IP[Hash client IP to server]
    RR --> S1[Server 1]
    RR --> S2[Server 2]
    RR --> S3[Server 3]
    LC --> S1
    LC --> S2
    LC --> S3
    IP --> S1
    IP --> S2
    IP --> S3
    style RR fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32
    style LC fill:#e3f2fd,stroke:#1565c0
    style IP fill:#fff3e0,stroke:#ef6c00

data.title: When to use each algorithm
items: Use round robin for uniform, short-lived requests.
Use least connections when request duration varies significantly.
Use IP hash when you need simple session stickiness without shared session storage.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Round robin is simple but ignores server load.
Least connections adapts to variable request duration.
IP hash provides session locality at the cost of scaling flexibility.
data.takeaway: Algorithm choice should match workload characteristics and scaling behavior.
